chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Uqbah ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the person in ihram entering the bathhouse. He said: 'He does not enter.' The meaning in this report is that we should interpret it as a form of dislike (karahah) rather than prohibition (haram), and the first report as permissible, removing the prohibition.

key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةِ: Dislike (a legal status less severe than prohibition)
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمِ: The person in the state of ihram (ritual consecration)

ai.seo_question: Is it forbidden for a person in ihram to take a bath?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq clarifies that the entry of a person in *ihram* into a bathhouse is not strictly prohibited (*haram*) but rather disliked (*karahat*), resolving apparent contradictions in earlier reports. This reflects the Shia juristic principle of distinguishing between absolute prohibition and mere dislike, allowing for flexibility in ritual purity practices during pilgrimage.
